question: A patient with multiple sclerosis develops lower limb spasticity with painful muscle spasms. Which drug class is appropriate, and why are neuromuscular blocking drugs unsuitable?

answers.text: Centrally acting spasmolytics (baclofen, tizanidine) — they reduce spinal cord hyperexcitability while preserving voluntary motor control; NMBDs would cause complete paralysis requiring ventilation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Spasticity is an upper motor neuron disorder requiring reduction of spinal cord excitability. Baclofen (GABA-B agonist) and tizanidine (central α2 agonist) achieve this while preserving consciousness and partial voluntary movement. NMBDs cause complete flaccid paralysis at the NMJ — the patient would need mechanical ventilation.

answers.text: Non-depolarising NMBDs at low doses — they safely relax muscles without requiring ventilation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no safe 'low dose' NMBD for ambulatory use. NMBDs block all neuromuscular transmission — partial blockade is unpredictable, and any diaphragmatic involvement compromises breathing. These are exclusively operating-theatre drugs.

answers.text: Succinylcholine — its short duration allows intermittent dosing for chronic spasticity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Succinylcholine causes fasciculations followed by complete paralysis, is painful, carries hyperkalaemia risk with repeated doses, and requires airway management. It has absolutely no role in chronic spasticity.

answers.text: Dantrolene — first-line for all types of chronic spasticity due to its peripheral mechanism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Dantrolene acts peripherally on RyR1 and can reduce tone, but it carries significant hepatotoxicity with long-term use. It is reserved for malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not first-line chronic spasticity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key concept: spasticity is managed centrally (baclofen, tizanidine) to reduce spinal hyperexcitability while preserving voluntary movement. NMBDs cause complete paralysis requiring ventilation — entirely inappropriate for ambulatory care.
Well done. The distinction between NMJ blockade (paralysis) and central spinal modulation (spasticity reduction) is the foundation of safe muscle relaxant prescribing.
